messages.author: fd4f3538f907404b
messages.subject: knitr -> LaTeX -> HTML
parts:
I am getting closer in my quest to convert knitr-style Sweave -> LaTeX
-> HTML in a clean way. (I know Yihui and a lot of power users here
would prefer to use Markdown as a starting point, and that makes sense a
lot of the time -- but I have some fairly complicated documents that I
really do want to use LaTeX+R chunks (rather than Markdown+R chunks) to
write, and I would still like to produce HTML as an alternative output
format to PDF ...)

Here's a sample document that shows how far I've gotten:

http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.Rnw
http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.html
http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/bolker/misc/knitr_listings_test.pdf

This is using render_listings() as advised by Yihui, and using htlatex
to convert from LaTeX to HTML.

My only problems at the moment (with this very simple document --
perhaps I will have more trouble with something more complex ...) are

(1) htlatex chokes slightly on the '<-' expression inside S input chunks
-- it does give the right output in the end, and I can hit 's' to skip
over errors, but if possible it would be nice to figure out how to make
the errors go away.

(2) the HTML output isn't very beautiful -- tried to fix this with some
CSS magic found in one of the links referred to in my document, but no
luck yet.

(3) I prefer the native syntax highlighting generated in 'standard'
knitr to the render_listings()-style output (but this is looking a gift
horse in the mouth, and I can certainly live with it.

I realize this is pretty obscure, but maybe someone has an idea (and
maybe this will be useful to someone else). I'm a little out of my
depth in dealing with the multiple layers here [knitr/listings
package/htlatex] (I haven't cc'd Frank Harrell on this because I don't
want to bug him, but Frank, if you're reading this, I can imagine that
you would have some ideas ...)

thanks
Ben Bolker

[ snip ]

I have a similar quest:

1. Write once!. I don't care what the initial authoring format is (LyX
or Markdown, for example) as long as I have a reasonable continuous
integration workflow. I write and my "reproducible research"
compendium of code, text and data is continuously built and tested and
the output documents continuously updated and viewable.

2. Four outputs that pass validation suites and that look good: PDF,
EPUB, MOBI and HTML5 with all the bells and whistles, interactivity,
etc.. Again, this must all be automated in the tradition of
reproducible research. The ideal case would be an HTML5 full-featured
output as the "prime" document with the others derived from it by a
mechanical reduction process.

3. Ability to mix R with Perl and bash scripts in the compendium. Most
everything is in R, but I have quite a bit of Twitter interface code
that uses Perl and quite a few bash scripts that install OS-level
dependencies.

I'm almost there (on Fedora Linux; Windows is hopeless, I can't afford
a Mac and no matter which Linux I pick, some components need to be
built from source rather than from the distro's repositories). I write
now in LyX and run a bash script using ImageMagick, Sigil, epubcheck
and Calibre "every so often" to export LyX to PDF and HTML and then do
the EPUB / MOBI reformatting. The document is currently using "knitr",
not "Sweave". There are a few manual steps in this but I'm pretty sure
they can be automated, or at least won't be so annoying when I have a
continuous integration toolchain.

I'm hoping to migrate this to RStudio / Markdown this week and
complete the continuous integration coding. There's little reason not
to do the continuous integration and test code in R. It's not as
"pretty" as Ruby, Python, Perl or bash but it will do the job.

The two stumbling blocks are

1. RStudio "knit to HTML" embeds the image as a Base64 object directly
in the HTML. I'm sure there's a "hook" to get it into its own file,
but I haven't found it yet. I need the image separate because it needs
to be full-size in the PDF and HTML5 output but scaled down via
ImageMagick for the EPUB and MOBI.

2. There doesn't seem to be a "knit to HTML *and* PDF". The best I've
found so far is to generate an Rnw as an intermediate.

I think I can do most of this with hooks, but I'm looking at some
other tools that seem to have more built-in infrastructure. My
preference is to acquire code rather than write it. ;-)

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knitr -> LaTeX -> HTML
parts:
1. You can probably redefine the Rstyle by stopping <- from being
replaced by a real arrow in Sweavel.sty:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/misc/Sweavel.sty#L42

Or you can put a copy of Sweavel.sty in your working directory and
remove the part that replaces <- with a left arrow. That part came
from Frank, I believe.

2. I cannot help much here.

3. The best approach to do syntax highlighting in the web is probably
highlight.js, which is agnostic of languages; you just need to put
code in <pre></pre>. It is pretty neat. But the HTML code generated
from LaTeX is a real mess, so there is no hope... Yes, markdown is
much cleaner... and the best friend of LaTeX is always PDF...

Regards,
Yihui

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knitr -> LaTeX -> HTML
parts:
In theory you can write any languages in knitr besides R. There are
some which are already supported like Python, Ruby, Awk, Bash, ... I
have a series of hello world examples under
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/

For example,

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/027-engine-bash.Rmd
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/027-engine-bash.md

https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/023-engine-python.Rmd
https://github.com/yihui/knitr-examples/blob/master/023-engine-python.md

For your stumbling blocks:

1. You can customize how markdown is converted to HTML in RStudio, but
I do not really like the way of customization:
http://www.rstudio.org/docs/authoring/markdown_custom_rendering

I will probably talk to them later, but anyway, you can define your
own converter to ignore the base64 encoding step.

2. Again, you can define a custom converter to do that. Markdown to
PDF is not a natural conversion, although Pandoc has done a lot of
work. HTML lives best in the web browser, and PDF is best for
printing. For example, you do not need to worry about pages in the web
browser (because everything is in one continuous page), but that is a
big challenge when you do typesetting in PDF.

I understand people tend to be greedy (write one and generate all),
but there is just no free lunch :) We have to make a decision on which
output format is primary and which is secondary.

Regards,
Yihui
--

messages.author: ca3205004f4bea24
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] knitr -> LaTeX -> HTML
parts:
On Fri, Aug 10, 2012 at 12:16 PM, Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com> wrote:

> 3. The best approach to do syntax highlighting in the web is probably
> highlight.js, which is agnostic of languages; you just need to put
> code in <pre></pre>. It is pretty neat. But the HTML code generated
> from LaTeX is a real mess, so there is no hope... Yes, markdown is
> much cleaner... and the best friend of LaTeX is always PDF...

The HTML coming out of LyX 2.0.4 "Export" isn't too bad - I've been
able to push it into Sigil and Calibre and make EPUB and MOBI eBooks
using ImageMagick to resize the images. A good HTML parser / rewrite
algorithm wouldn't be too difficult to add, there's always Bluefish,
and you can make PDFs from HTML without too much difficulty.

Like it or not, HTML5 / CSS3 / Chrome-Firefox JavaScript *are* the
languages we need to know to publish in 2012, *not* LaTeX or Markdown.
Markdown is IMHO a coders' way of distracting themselves from the task
at hand, producing reproducible research/analyses/reports. The fact
that there are half a dozen incompatible dialects of Markdown tells me
that it is just that - a distraction.
